checks.prompt: A company has a large existing service with well-tested business logic, strict logging and authorisation requirements, and a mandate to be able to move between model providers without a rewrite. They want the model to be able to call a subset of the existing logic. A second team wants a quick document-question prototype over a folder of PDFs. Which team is this SDK aimed at, and what specifically makes the difference?
checks.explanation: This is an application framework's answer to putting a model inside a real system: a container holding model connectors and plugins, so your existing code is exposed as capabilities a model can call, the provider is a registration detail rather than a rewrite, and logging, authorisation and caching attach as hooks around invocations rather than being sprinkled through call sites. That ceremony is exactly what a quick retrieval prototype does not want — there a thin pipeline or the raw provider SDK is fewer moving parts. And the plan-assembling components the last option describes are legacy; the current idiom is the model choosing tools directly.
options: The first. Its organising abstraction is a container into which you register model connectors and named collections of callable functions, so existing code becomes callable capabilities, provider changes are a registration change, and cross-cutting concerns attach as hooks around every invocation. The second team wants a short retrieval pipeline, where a thin composition library or the provider's own SDK is less ceremony for the same result
The second. The SDK's strength is prebuilt retrieval and document handling, whereas exposing existing code to a model requires a lower-level agent graph
Both equally: the container is a thin wrapper, so the prototype gains provider-agnosticism at no cost and the enterprise app gains a retrieval pipeline it will need eventually
Neither: the SDK is a planner that assembles multi-step plans, so it suits neither a code-integration problem nor a retrieval prototype

checks.prompt: Explain this SDK's central abstraction by analogy to a dependency-injection container in a conventional web application. Name the things you register and what each is for, describe the two kinds of function it can hold and what makes them uniform, and explain what happens when the model is allowed to choose. Then explain the sentence 'everything the model can do is a registered function, and everything you register the model can be allowed to call' — including the security consequence.
checks.expected: A correct answer must carry the container analogy: as a web application has a service container holding the components it depends on, here there is one small container holding model connectors and capabilities, and it also acts as a dispatcher for invocations. What is registered must be enumerated: model services or connectors — a chat-completion backend, an embedding backend — which are swappable so that changing provider is a registration change rather than a rewrite; plugins, which are named bundles of related functions and are the unit of capability the model sees; and hooks that wrap invocations for cross-cutting concerns like logging, authorisation, caching and redaction. The two kinds of function must be distinguished: native functions are ordinary code marked with a decorator, whose type hints and description become the schema a model reads; prompt functions are a template plus a model, so the implementation IS the model call. Uniformity is the point — both are invoked the same way, so a prompt template can call a native function and native code can invoke a prompt function. Letting the model choose must be described as handing it the catalogue of registered functions and executing whatever it picks, looping until the work is done — the modern replacement for the older components that asked a model to pre-assemble a plan. The final sentence must be unpacked in both directions, and the security consequence stated: the catalogue is the boundary of what the model can do, so what you register is an authorisation decision, and anything registered is potentially reachable by model-generated intent — which is why hooks that authorise and log invocations, and registering only the functions a given surface should expose, matter. Noting that descriptions and type hints are an API contract read by the model rather than comments is a plus.

checks.prompt: A team's model keeps calling the wrong capability. Their functions are registered and the calls execute correctly when invoked directly from code. Their descriptions read like internal comments — one says 'legacy path, see ticket 4412' — and several parameters have no type hints. A second issue: after adding a second model service, their execution settings stopped finding a model. What are the two causes?
checks.explanation: When the model picks the tools, the catalogue is the entire basis for its decision, and the catalogue is built from what you wrote: the description on each function and the parameter type hints. Treating those as comments rather than as the contract is the reliable way to get the wrong function called or none at all. The second is a small but common wiring detail: services are registered under an identifier, and execution settings reference that identifier — with more than one service registered, a mismatch means there is no model to route the call to.
options: With the model choosing, selection is driven entirely by the catalogue built from each function's description and parameter type hints — so an internal note and untyped parameters give the model nothing to select on; those strings are the contract the model reads. The second is that execution settings reference a service by its registered identifier, so once more than one is registered a mismatched identifier means the kernel cannot resolve which model to use

Selection is by function name only, so descriptions are irrelevant and the fix is renaming the functions; the second issue means the second service replaced the first, and services must be registered in a single call
The model is choosing from the plan produced by the planner component, so descriptions matter only if a planner is configured; the second issue is that two services require two kernels
Wrong selection means automatic choice is disabled and calls are falling back to the first registered function; the second issue is unrelated churn in import paths

checks.prompt: Build the container and dispatcher. Write a decorator `kernel_function(description="", name=None)` that marks a method callable and records the description and an exposed name defaulting to the Python name. Write a `Kernel` class with: `add_service(service_id, service)`; `add_plugin(instance, plugin_name)`, which collects every MARKED method of the instance into `self.plugins[plugin_name]` keyed by exposed name and returns that mapping; `add_filter(fn)`; `catalog()`, returning a list of `{"plugin", "name", "description", "parameters"}` dicts sorted by plugin then function name, where `parameters` maps each declared parameter (excluding `self`, which a bound method does not expose) to its type annotation's `__name__`, or `"string"` when unannotated; `invoke(plugin_name, function_name, **kwargs)`, raising `KeyError` for an unknown plugin or function and otherwise calling the function through the registered filters, each of which has the signature `(plugin_name, function_name, args_dict, next_fn)` and is free to inspect or replace the arguments, call `next_fn(args)`, return a value without calling it, or raise — the FIRST-registered filter being the outermost; `render(template, **args)`, replacing each `{{$name}}` with the matching argument's string form, leaving a `{{$name}}` with no matching argument as literal text, and replacing each `{{plugin.function}}` with the string form of invoking that no-argument function; and `auto_invoke(goal, chooser, max_calls=5)`, which repeatedly calls `chooser(goal, self.catalog(), <the calls made so far>)` — each returning either None to stop or a `(plugin, function, args)` triple to invoke through `invoke` — recording `{"plugin", "name", "args", "result"}` per call, stopping at None or at `max_calls`, and returning the list. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: Read the catalogue assertions first: what the model sees is the description you wrote and the parameter types you declared, which is why those are an API contract and not documentation — and note that an undecorated method is simply not a capability, so exposure is a deliberate act. The template assertions show the two halves of the uniform surface: variables substitute, a registered function can be called from inside a prompt, and a mistyped variable renders as literal text rather than raising, which is exactly why a strange-looking answer means printing the rendered prompt. The filter block is the enterprise story made concrete: the same hook mechanism gives you audit logging, an authorisation check that refuses a call, and a cache that answers without ever running the function — none of which required touching a plugin. Finally, the model-driven loop runs through that same invocation path, so those hooks apply to model-chosen calls too, and it is bounded on purpose, because a model may keep chaining calls and each one costs.
checks.test:
class MathPlugin:
    @kernel_function(description="Add two integers")
    def add(self, a: int, b: int) -> int:
        return a + b

    @kernel_function(description="Square an integer", name="sq")
    def square(self, x: int) -> int:
        return x * x

    def helper(self, x):
        return x


class TextPlugin:
    @kernel_function(description="Shout the text in upper case")
    def shout(self, text: str) -> str:
        return text.upper() + "!"


kernel = Kernel()
kernel.add_service("chat", lambda prompt: f"MODEL<{prompt}>")
kernel.add_plugin(MathPlugin(), plugin_name="math")
kernel.add_plugin(TextPlugin(), plugin_name="text")

assert kernel.invoke("math", "add", a=40, b=2) == 42
assert kernel.invoke("text", "shout", text="hi") == "HI!"
# The decorator's name argument is what the model sees, not the Python name.
assert kernel.invoke("math", "sq", x=9) == 81
assert "square" not in kernel.plugins["math"]
# An undecorated method is not a capability, so it is not exposed at all.
assert "helper" not in kernel.plugins["math"]

# The catalog IS the tool schema: the description and the parameter types are what
# a model reads when deciding what to call, so they are an API contract.
catalog = kernel.catalog()
assert [(e["plugin"], e["name"]) for e in catalog] == \
    [("math", "add"), ("math", "sq"), ("text", "shout")], catalog
add_entry = catalog[0]
assert add_entry["description"] == "Add two integers", add_entry
assert add_entry["parameters"] == {"a": "int", "b": "int"}, add_entry
assert "self" not in add_entry["parameters"], add_entry
assert catalog[2]["parameters"] == {"text": "str"}, catalog[2]

for bad in (("nope", "add"), ("math", "divide")):
    try:
        kernel.invoke(*bad)
    except KeyError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError(f"{bad} must be refused")

# Templates substitute their variables...
assert kernel.render("Explain {{$topic}} to a child.", topic="a kernel") == \
    "Explain a kernel to a child."
assert kernel.render("{{$a}}+{{$a}}", a=1) == "1+1"
# ...a mistyped variable renders as literal text rather than raising, which is why
# an odd-looking answer means checking the rendered prompt.
assert kernel.render("Explain {{$topik}}.", topic="x") == "Explain {{$topik}}."
# ...and a template may call a registered function, which is what makes prompts and
# code one uniform surface.

class Zero:
    @kernel_function(description="Always 42")
    def answer(self) -> int:
        return 42


kernel.add_plugin(Zero(), plugin_name="const")
assert kernel.render("The answer is {{const.answer}}.") == "The answer is 42."
assert kernel.render("{{const.answer}} and {{$x}}", x="y") == "42 and y"

# Filters wrap every invocation, in registration order, and see the call before it
# happens -- which is how logging, authorisation and caching are added without
# touching a single function.
log = []
audited = Kernel()
audited.add_plugin(MathPlugin(), plugin_name="math")
audited.add_filter(lambda p, f, args, nxt: (log.append(f"outer {p}.{f}"), nxt(args))[1])
audited.add_filter(lambda p, f, args, nxt: (log.append(f"inner {f}{args}"), nxt(args))[1])
assert audited.invoke("math", "add", a=1, b=2) == 3
assert log == ["outer math.add", "inner add{'a': 1, 'b': 2}"], log

# A filter may refuse a call outright...
blocked = Kernel()
blocked.add_plugin(MathPlugin(), plugin_name="math")


def deny(plugin, function, args, nxt):
    if function == "add":
        raise PermissionError("not allowed")
    return nxt(args)


blocked.add_filter(deny)
try:
    blocked.invoke("math", "add", a=1, b=1)
except PermissionError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("a filter must be able to refuse")
assert blocked.invoke("math", "sq", x=3) == 9

# ...or answer without calling the function at all, which is caching.
ran = []
cached = Kernel()


class Slow:
    @kernel_function(description="expensive")
    def work(self, n: int) -> int:
        ran.append(n)
        return n * 10


cached.add_plugin(Slow(), plugin_name="slow")
store = {}


def memo(plugin, function, args, nxt):
    key = (function, tuple(sorted(args.items())))
    if key not in store:
        store[key] = nxt(args)
    return store[key]


cached.add_filter(memo)
assert [cached.invoke("slow", "work", n=2) for _ in range(3)] == [20, 20, 20]
assert ran == [2], ran

# Letting the model choose: it reads the catalog and the kernel runs what it picks,
# through the same path -- so the filters above apply to model-chosen calls too.
def chooser(goal, catalog, so_far):
    names = [(e["plugin"], e["name"]) for e in catalog]
    assert ("math", "add") in names
    if not so_far:
        return ("math", "add", {"a": 40, "b": 2})
    if len(so_far) == 1:
        return ("math", "sq", {"x": so_far[0]["result"]})
    return None


chained = kernel.auto_invoke("compute", chooser)
assert [c["name"] for c in chained] == ["add", "sq"], chained
assert chained[-1]["result"] == 42 * 42, chained

# The loop is bounded, because a model may chain calls indefinitely.
runaway = kernel.auto_invoke(
    "spin", lambda g, c, so_far: ("math", "add", {"a": 1, "b": 1}), max_calls=3)
assert len(runaway) == 3, runaway
assert kernel.auto_invoke("none", lambda g, c, s: None) == []

checks.prompt: A Python service using this SDK logs 'result: <coroutine object ...>' instead of an answer. After that is fixed, a monitoring dashboard shows one user request occasionally producing eleven model calls. The team is also following a tutorial that builds a multi-step plan from the registered functions before executing anything. Assess all three.
checks.explanation: Three unrelated things, each a real trap. The Python API is async-first, so a missing await hands you a coroutine object rather than a result. A single request producing many model calls is not a bug — when the model chooses tools it may chain several — but it is unbounded unless you bound it, which is what iteration caps and invocation hooks are for. And the plan-assembling components that older tutorials use are legacy: the current idiom is native tool-calling, where the model picks from the catalogue directly.
options: The logged coroutine is the async-first API: most invocations are coroutines and must be awaited inside an event loop, or you get the coroutine object rather than a result. The eleven calls are the model chaining tool calls within one request, which is expected behaviour that must be bounded — cap the iterations and use invocation hooks to log and limit calls, or cost creeps silently. And the tutorial is teaching a legacy component: pre-assembling a plan has largely been replaced by letting the model choose tools directly

The coroutine means the wrong connector was registered; the eleven calls indicate a retry loop caused by that same misregistration; and the plan-assembling component is the current recommended approach, so the tutorial is correct
All three come from version churn in the import paths: pinning the version resolves the coroutine, the call count and the deprecated component together
The coroutine is correct and should be logged as-is; the eleven calls mean automatic tool choice is disabled and each call is a separate request; the plan-assembling component is the fix for both

checks.prompt: Three situations. (a) A .NET line-of-business application that must expose thirty existing service methods to a model, log and authorise every model-initiated call, and switch providers by configuration. (b) A team that wants a research-and-write pipeline described as a small team of specialists, standing up in an afternoon. (c) A support agent whose control flow loops, branches on classification results, persists across sessions and pauses for human approval. Recommend for each with reasons, then say what the trade-off is in choosing this SDK when it is NOT the obvious fit.
checks.expected: A correct answer must place all three against the reasons. (a) This SDK: the requirements read as its feature list — a container registering existing code as callable capabilities, provider connectors making the switch a registration change, and hooks around invocations for authorisation and logging; the .NET target is also where the SDK is most mature. (b) A role-and-task pipeline framework: the job is described as specialists working a checklist and the goal is speed, which is what an opinionated higher-level framework buys; the trade is less control and a tendency for autonomy to wander. (c) A state-graph runtime: loops, branching on results, persistence across sessions and human approval gates are exactly what an explicit graph with state and checkpointing provides, and neither a container nor a role pipeline models them directly. The trade-off question must be answered concretely rather than as a preference: choosing this SDK when the problem is a quick retrieval chain or a one-off prompt buys ceremony you do not need — registration, async invocation, execution settings — where a thin composition pipeline or the provider's raw SDK would do; and it has less in the way of prebuilt multi-agent recipes than the role-based framework, plus real multi-language API churn to manage by pinning versions. A strong answer notes that these are not exclusive — the SDK also has higher-level agent and stateful-process layers, and the vendor's conversational multi-agent framework is converging with it — so the boundary is moving; and that the deciding question is whether the model is one component inside a larger application, which is when this abstraction pays.
